ui.home.h1: Image tools that never upload your files
ui.home.intro: Every tool here runs inside your own browser tab. Your images are processed on your device and are never sent to a server, because there is no server to send them to.
ui.home.howHeading: What happens when you use a tool
ui.home.howP1: You pick an image straight from your device. The page does the decoding, resizing and re-encoding right there in the tab — on a background Web Worker, wherever this browser offers one, so the page stays responsive — and your browser saves the result back to your device. Nothing is uploaded, nothing is queued, and closing the tab ends the whole thing.
ui.home.howP2: That means no sign-up, no file size limit imposed by a server, and no copies of your images sitting on someone else's disk. It also means the tools work offline once the page has loaded, and that a slow connection only affects how fast the page arrives — never how fast your images are processed.

ui.compress.unsupported: This browser cannot compress images locally — it is missing the image-decoding API these tools are built on. Nothing is uploaded either way. Please try a current version of Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari.
ui.compress.sliderLabel: Drag to compare the original and the compressed image
ui.compress.notesIntro: Your images are decoded and re-encoded right here in this browser tab — on a background Web Worker, where this browser offers one, so the page stays responsive — and the files never reach a server. There is no backend, no queue and no account.
ui.compress.notes1: The original files stay on your device from start to finish.
ui.compress.notes2: A target file size searches for the highest quality that fits under it, per image. If an image cannot get that small, you still get the smallest one we could make and a note saying so.
ui.compress.notes3: Max width and height shrink the pixel dimensions first, which often saves more bytes than quality alone.
ui.compress.notes4: Drop several images at once and the finished ones come back together in a single ZIP.
ui.compress.notes5: Nothing is stored: reloading the page discards everything.
ui.resize.unsupported: This browser cannot resize images locally — it is missing the image-decoding API these tools are built on. Nothing is uploaded either way. Please try a current version of Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari.
ui.resize.allowUpscale: Allow enlarging past the original size
ui.resize.sliderLabel: Drag to compare the original and the resized image
ui.resize.notesIntro: The resize happens right here in this browser tab — on a background Web Worker, where this browser offers one — using a Lanczos-style resampling filter, so edges stay smooth instead of going jaggy the way a cheap nearest-neighbour scale does. The image never reaches a server.
ui.resize.notes1: Preset sizes are real platform values, and each one is documented in the source with where it came from — YouTube asks for 3840×2160 for video thumbnails, for instance, not the 1280×720 people often repeat.
ui.resize.notes2: With the aspect ratio locked, the image scales to fit inside the box you type, so nothing is stretched. Unlock it to set an exact width and height.
ui.resize.notes3: Small images are left alone unless you tick Allow enlarging: interpolation can add pixels but not detail.
ui.resize.notes4: A batch resizes every image to the same box, then comes back as a single ZIP.
ui.resize.notes5: Nothing is stored: reloading the page discards everything.
ui.convert.unsupported: This browser cannot convert images locally — it is missing the image-decoding API these tools are built on. Nothing is uploaded either way. Please try a current version of Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari.
ui.convert.heicNote: That is a HEIC or HEIF file, the format iPhones and many cameras shoot by default. This browser cannot decode it natively, so a decoder is fetched from this site to read it — still on your device, still never uploaded.
ui.convert.sliderLabel: Drag to compare the original and the converted image
ui.convert.notesIntro: The image is decoded, redrawn and re-encoded right here in this browser tab — on a background Web Worker, where this browser offers one. Nothing is uploaded, and there is no file-size limit imposed by a server because there is no server.
ui.convert.notes1: The format list is built from what your browser can actually encode, tested at load time. A format the browser cannot write is not offered, rather than silently producing something else.
ui.convert.notes2: Converting to JPEG flattens transparency onto white, because JPEG has no alpha channel. The result panel says so when it happens.
ui.convert.notes3: HEIC and HEIF files from an iPhone work: Safari reads them directly, and other browsers fetch a small decoder that runs on your device.
ui.convert.notes4: A batch converts every image to the same format and returns them as one ZIP.
ui.convert.notes5: Re-encoding an already-optimised image can add a few bytes. The readout shows what actually happened rather than promising a saving.
ui.enhance.styleHint: Every thumbnail below is rendered from your own photo, not a sample. Picking one applies that style to the full-size image, and the intensity slider decides how far it goes.
ui.enhance.intensityHint: How far to push the style. At 0% you get the auto-corrected photo on its own, at 100% the full effect. It is disabled while Auto enhance is selected, because there is no style to blend towards.
ui.enhance.advancedHint: Manual overrides applied on top of whichever style is selected. Leave them at their defaults unless you want to fine-tune by hand.
ui.enhance.unsupported: This browser cannot enhance photos locally — it is missing the image-decoding API these tools are built on. Nothing is uploaded either way. Please try a current version of Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari.
ui.enhance.sliderLabel: Drag to compare the original photo with the enhanced one
ui.enhance.notesIntro: The photo is decoded, corrected, graded and re-encoded right here in this browser tab — on a background Web Worker, where this browser offers one. Nothing is uploaded, there is no queue on a server, and closing the page discards everything.
ui.enhance.notes1: First, a histogram correction. The tool finds the real black and white point of each colour channel, ignoring a small slice of outlier pixels so that one reflected highlight cannot set the range, then stretches what is left across the full range. Stretching the three channels independently is what removes a colour cast; the amount of stretch is capped, because amplifying a nearly black photo mostly amplifies its noise.
ui.enhance.notes2: Then a style. The five styles are applied on top of the corrected photo, and the intensity slider blends between the two — so a look that is too strong can always be dialled back to the corrected photo rather than to the original.
ui.enhance.notes3: The thumbnails are your own photo, rendered at 160 pixels wide by the same code that processes the full-size image. A style you have not seen applied to your picture is a style you cannot really choose.
ui.enhance.notes4: Keep the original dimensions or upscale 2×/4× with bicubic resampling. Choose JPG, PNG or WebP. Upscaling cannot recover detail absent from the original.
ui.enhance.notes5: Drop several photos and the whole batch is enhanced with the same style and returned as one ZIP. The style still applies to the pixels on your device, one image at a time.

ui.crop.notesIntro: You drag the selection over the image, then the crop is drawn and re-encoded right here in this browser tab — on a background Web Worker, where this browser offers one. The original file is never modified and never uploaded — cropping produces a new file for you to download.
ui.crop.notes1: Pick an aspect ratio to keep the selection to a fixed shape, or leave it free and drag any rectangle.
ui.crop.notes2: Rotate in 90° steps and flip across or down if the photo is the wrong way round. Rotating by a quarter turn swaps the output's width and height.
ui.crop.notes3: The crop is applied at full resolution — the selection is a view of the pixels, not a downscale of them.

ui.pdf.notes4: PNG is embedded directly. Other formats are re-encoded as JPEG, with orientation applied and a white background behind transparency.
